documents.abstract: This thesis examines the psychological nature, components, and causes of academic burnout among students. Academic burnout is interpreted as a consequence of an imbalance between academic demands and personal resources. The factors that play an important role in its prevention, including self-regulation, self-efficacy, social support, intrinsic motivation, and teacher–student relationships, are analyzed. Furthermore, the main directions of psychological and pedagogical prevention are systematized.

Generative artificial intelligence is being applied to create music in an ever-widening range, but it has not been determined whether the results can effectively convey human emotions. A controlled-variable experimental design is used to explore the causal relationship between information density in prompts and listeners' affective recognition of AI-generated music. Six AI-generated musical works were selected as the experimental stimuli under three increasing levels of prompt conditions: minimal emotional descriptions, prompts that added harmonic progression information, and detailed prompts including parameters such as instrumentation, vocal processing and dynamic changes. The results showed that listeners could not understand the creators' purposes in either the minimal-prompt or harmony-augmented situations. All 30 listeners were able to feel the emotion and structure that were desired, and they could do so after repeated instructions. The study also found that the audio outputs of AI music systems generally have logical discontinuities and perceptual incongruity without fine-grained human encoding intervention. This paper proposes that AI functions as a medium for music creation, and its affective communication performance is based on a closed-loop human intervention system at two stages: prompt engineering (information encoding) and generative evaluation (signal decoding). This study offers empirical support and practical paths for human-AI collaboration models in AI-assisted music creation.

The rapid advancement of artificial intelligence has significantly influenced contemporary educational practices, offering opportunities to enhance teaching and learning while raising concerns about effective and ethical integration. This study examines AI utilization and user satisfaction among science teachers and students, and analyzes its effects on satisfaction, usefulness, ease of use, and reliability. A quantitative research design involved 242 STEM students and 22 science teachers in the Division of Tacurong City. Data were collected through structured questionnaires and analyzed using descriptive statistics and Structural Equation Modeling. Results showed high AI utilization among students (x̄ = 3.79) and very high utilization among teachers (x̄ = 4.21). Satisfaction was high among students (x̄ = 3.87) and very high among teachers (x̄ = 4.38). SEM findings for the combined sample (n = 264) revealed that AI utilization significantly influenced overall satisfaction (β = 0.465, R² = 0.217, p < .001), usefulness (β = 0.457, R² = 0.208, p < .001), ease of use (β = 0.336, R² = 0.113, p < .001), and reliability (β = 0.257, R² = 0.066, p < .001). Among students (n = 242), AI utilization also showed significant positive effects on satisfaction and all dimensions. Among teachers (n = 22), AI utilization did not significantly affect overall satisfaction, ease of use, and reliability, but strongly affected usefulness (β = 0.576, R² = 0.332, p = .005). The findings indicate that AI is widely utilized and positively perceived among science teachers and students.

Artificial intelligence has become increasingly prominent in corporate disclosure, yet firms' AI-related narratives may not always be supported by observable investment in technology or human capital. Using AI-related keywords from annual reports, AI patents, and AI-related job postings of Chinese A-share firms from 2020 to 2025, we construct a firm-year measure to examine this disclosure-investment gap. We classify a firm as an AI washer when its AI-related disclosure is above the industry-year median, while both AI patent activity and AI-related recruitment remain below their corresponding medians. Firms meeting this definition are associated with lower annual stock returns, and the result remains qualitatively unchanged when we use alternative methods to identify AI patents. Additional tests point to two related market responses: AI washing is accompanied by more negative media coverage and weaker investor sentiment. The return discount is also more pronounced among firms with higher institutional ownership and among firms in regions with stronger local AI policy support. These results suggest that investors do not treat AI-related disclosure independently of observable corporate activity. Instead, the impact of AI narratives on stock returns appears to depend partly on whether firms can support those narratives with technological development and hiring.

Artificial intelligence is increasingly embedded in modern military operations, influencing how commanders interpret sensor data, assess threats, and make rapid decisions under pressure. While AI improves situational awareness and accelerates operational tempo, it also introduces vulnerabilities such as fabricated outputs, misclassifications, and opaque decision processes. Human factors—including stress, uncertainty, and organisational pressure—further complicate decision reliability, especially in compressed timelines. This article uses a SWOT analysis to evaluate the strengths, weaknesses, opportunities, and threats associated with AI‑enabled battlefield decision-making. It also examines how human judgment interacts with AI recommendations and identifies doctrinal and oversight mechanisms needed to preserve stability in modern conflict environments.

Artificial intelligence creates opportunities for students with visual impairments to access learning materials in adaptable formats, obtain descriptions of visual information, and receive support that responds to their pace of interaction. The availability of an application, however, does not constitute accessibility. This study analyses the dimensions of accessibility, the barriers that emerge, and the conditions required for meaningful participation in such learning. A qualitative descriptive approach was employed through thematic document analysis of 23 sources, comprising 19 scholarly articles published between 2022 and 2026 and four policy or accessibility-standard documents. The analysis yields a five-layer framework: operability; informational equivalence and modality flexibility; output reliability and verifiability; user competence and pedagogical mediation; and governance and infrastructure. Artificial intelligence can strengthen learning independence, yet it also generates new barriers: unlabeled controls, loss of meaning in visual materials, inaccurate outputs, bias, privacy risks, and unequal access to devices. The framework is offered as an initial audit reference requiring field validation.
topics: Assistive Technology in Communication and Mobility

documents.abstract: With the continuous development of artificial intelligence (AI) technology, smart home systems have gradually evolved from traditional automated control modes toward intelligent systems with environmental perception, autonomous decision-making, and proactive service capabilities. However, existing smart homes still face problems such as a single mode of interaction, insufficient intelligent proactivity, and limited scene adaptability. Based on relevant research results in recent years, this paper systematically reviews the application progress of AI technology in the smart home field, focusing on key directions such as the Internet of Things (IoT) architecture, multimodal interaction, intelligent decision-making, edge computing, and data security. The review shows that AI technology has effectively improved the perception, interaction, and decision-making capabilities of smart home systems. Among these technologies, large language models (LLMs) enhance natural language understanding and user interaction capabilities, edge computing improves the real-time response efficiency of the system, and technologies such as blockchain provide new solutions for data security. At the same time, smart homes still face challenges in privacy protection, model reliability, cross-device collaboration, and standardization. In the future, modern smart home systems should be further integrated with artificial intelligence technologies, change traditional basic interaction modes, and promote the development of smart homes toward greater intelligence, security, and adaptability.

Relevance. The increasing use of artificial intelligence (AI) assistants in professional settings introduces new forms of human–technology interaction. Perceiving an AI assistant as a human-like partner may be associated with users' confidence in their abilities and various aspects of occupational well-being. Objective. To examine the associations between perceived AI assistant anthropomorphism and employees' confidence in using AI, occupational self-efficacy, and two dimensions of occupational burnout: exhaustion and disengagement from work. Methods. Data from a cross-sectional online survey were analyzed. The initial dataset comprised 704 responses, of which 665 participants met the eligibility criteria for employment and regular AI use. After excluding four respondents who failed both attention checks, the final analytical sample consisted of 661 participants. The mean age was 30.06 years (SD = 7.34). Measures included the Godspeed, AISES, OSS, and OLBI scales. Descriptive statistics, internal consistency estimates, correlation analyses, and regression models were calculated. The interaction between perceived anthropomorphism and prior experience with AI was also examined. Results. The anthropomorphism measure (GOD_A) was positively correlated with the AI assistance and self-efficacy measure (AISES_AS; r = 0.148, 95% CI [0.073, 0.222], p < 0.001). Correlations with exhaustion (r = −0.010, p = 0.792) and disengagement (r = 0.024, p = 0.540) were not statistically significant. After controlling for AI use experience, age, and workload, the GOD_A coefficient in the AISES_AS regression model was β = 0.070 (p = 0.082). A statistically significant interaction between anthropomorphism and AI use experience was identified (b = 0.114, 95% CI [0.037, 0.191], p = 0.004). Conclusions. Perceived AI assistant anthropomorphism is associated with employees' confidence in using AI, with the nature of this association varying according to prior experience with the technology. No statistically significant direct association was identified between anthropomorphism and occupational burnout. These findings provide a foundation for further investigation into the psychological dimensions of AI implementation in organizational settings.

Unintentional falls among older adults represent a severe global health concern, necessitating reliable, automated wearable Fall Detection Systems (FDS). However, developing practical wearable solutions requires navigating intricate engineering trade-offs among diagnostic accuracy, power consumption, memory footprint, and software development overhead. This paper presents a structured hardware selection guide evaluating three representative embedded design paradigms: low-cost threshold logic on 8-bit microcontrollers (Profile A), balanced classical machine learning on standard 32-bit platforms (Profile B), and compressed on-chip TinyML neural networks on edge-capable microcontrollers (Profile C). Comparative analysis reveals that while threshold methods achieve multi-week battery longevity at sub-$12 costs, they suffer from high false-alarm rates during dynamic daily activities. Conversely, TinyML architectures deliver superior classification accuracy (98%) on raw kinematic streams, but introduce steep memory quantization barriers, complex toolchains, and shorter battery recharge intervals. Classical machine learning emerges as the optimal design compromise for most developers, achieving robust diagnostic discrimination (95% sensitivity and specificity) with manageable computational demands at $15-$25. Finally, this review evaluates sensor placement ergonomics, addresses pervasive demographic bias in youth-simulated training datasets, and delivers a practical hardware selection framework for student researchers and independent developers.
topics: Wireless Sensor Networks for Data Analysis

documents.abstract: The diffusion of digital technologies has shifted brand marketing from mass communication toward individualized consumer dialogue, and personalization has become a central capability for competitive differentiation. This paper examines how global brands design and implement personalization strategies in digital marketing environments, using L'Oréal, the world's largest cosmetics group, as a case. Drawing on a qualitative, single-case design and secondary data, including corporate reports, press releases, and peer-reviewed research, the study analyzes L'Oréal's personalization initiatives across four dimensions: data infrastructure and artificial intelligence (AI)-based diagnostics, augmented reality (AR) virtual try-on services, omnichannel customer relationship management, and personalized content delivered through influencers and social platforms. The findings indicate that L'Oréal's approach rests on proprietary technology ownership, systematic integration of AI and AR into the consumer journey, and organizational structures that connect data science with brand management. The case also reveals tensions involving privacy, algorithmic bias, and digital exclusion that condition the effectiveness of personalization. The study contributes an integrated framework that links AI capabilities to personalization touchpoints and brand outcomes, and offers managerial guidance for consumer goods firms seeking to scale personalization without eroding consumer trust.
topics: Consumer Behavior in Brand Consumption and Identification

documents.abstract: This paper presents the evolving concept of authorship in music creation as algorithmic and artificial intelligence systems impact the musical market. Based on Philip Galanter's definition of generative art, the paper discusses about the authorship of music in different senerios: when it is generated by tools like Nyquist or AI models such as Suno. The argument is structured around three distinct ways of human-machine interaction: human-led creation where computers are used as instruments; human-guided creation, where algorithms are restricted to a predetermined range of randomness; and human-crafted prompts, where AI generates the music completely. Following the analysis of these cases and some complex instances, this paper concludes that authorship is decided by the location of creativity and intentionality rather than a fixed attribute. The analysis reveals that authorship belongs to different subjects accordingly to different methods humans used to use generative tools: following the primary source of meaning contribution. Ultimately, the paper argues that the central issue may not be the authorship itself, but the human need for music to serve as a bridge for shared meaning and emotional connection.

With the increasing urban rail transit network and the closer connection among operational subsystems, the potential influence range and management difficulty of emergencies have greatly increased. The current emergency management based on traditional methods has some shortcomings in real-time risk recognition, integration of multi-source information and cross-departmental collaborative decision-making. By integrating a comprehensive literature survey with typical case analyses, this paper investigates the use of Internet of Things (IoT), big data, artificial intelligence (AI) and digital twins (DTs) in urban rail transit emergency management. The research is carried out from three main aspects: risk monitoring and early warning, emergency decision-making and collaborative response, and passenger evacuation and operation recovery. The results show that intelligent techniques offer assistance in the monitoring of operational status, anomaly detection, emergency information exchange and evaluation of evacuation plans, which can effectively improve the processing efficiency of information and the supportive ability in decision-making. However, at present, the actual implementations are limited by insufficient data sharing between different systems, restricted model generalization, lack of validation in practical operational situations, and network and data security risks. In the future, more efforts should be made to standardize multi-source data and sharing mechanisms, strengthen the validation of intelligent models and DT systems under real operational conditions, and optimize human-in-the-loop collaborative decision-making to improve the reliability and practicability of intelligent technologies in urban rail transit emergency management.

The rapid adoption of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in advertising since 2022 has transformed content production while raising concerns about the preservation of brand authenticity, a critical foundation of consumer trust and brand relationships. This study examines how AI-generated advertising influences perceived brand authenticity, identifies the mechanisms driving authenticity erosion, and explains the contextual factors that account for inconsistent findings in prior research. Following PRISMA 2020 guidelines, this review synthesizes 13 studies published between 2022 and 2026 retrieved from the Web of Science Core Collection and EBSCOhost databases. Through thematic synthesis, this study identifies three interrelated mechanisms through which AI-generated advertising may undermine brand authenticity: disclosure effects, failed anthropomorphism, and sincerity erosion. The findings further reveal that the effects of AI-generated advertising on authenticity perceptions are contingent upon individual characteristics, product and brand contexts, and source-related factors, including AI capability beliefs, product type, luxury positioning, and communicator characteristics. This study develops an integrated framework explaining when and why AI-generated advertising enhances or undermines brand authenticity, thus providing theoretical insights for consumer research and practical implications for AI-enabled marketing decision-making.
topics: Consumer Behavior in Brand Consumption and Identification

documents.abstract: In archaeological scholarship, the challenge of interpreting large amounts of fragmented evidence can be daunting. This paper will examine how artificial intelligence can assist in this process, mainly through examining visual evidence and classifying material evidence. Drawing from Trevor Paglen's argument of machine vision and Matteo Pasquinelli's history of classification in machines, this paper develops an analysis of two archaeological case studies: archaeological site detection based on satellite imagery in Mesopotamia and deep-learning classification of Tusayan White Ware pottery. The findings of the studies demonstrate that artificial intelligence is capable of expanding preliminary surveys as well as applying typologies consistently. At the same time, they also highlight the importance of human input, coming to the conclusion that artificial intelligence's potential and principal contribution lies in simplifying the archaeological process and directing human attention towards evidence requiring further interpretation, establishing a framework for understanding artificial intelligence as an assistive technology.

This research explores secondary education teachers" perceptions regarding the integration of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) into instructional practice. Through semi-structured interviews with a sample of ten (10) educators from diverse academic backgrounds, the study examines three core pillars: interaction and usability, issues of trust and ethics, and the transformation of professional identity. The findings reveal that using AI tools is a complex cognitive process requiring strategic prompt engineering. Despite the small sample size, participants consistently demonstrated a "cautious acceptance," acting as critical evaluators of machine-generated outputs to mitigate scientific inaccuracies and "hallucinations." In conclusion, the study highlights a shift in the teaching role from being a source of knowledge to an authority of critical mediation. It emphasizes the urgent need for professional development that fosters pedagogical agency and ethical action within the modern digital learning environment.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: This study aimed to synthesize, develop, and evaluate the Micro Game-Based Learning Model on Intelligent Metaverse Learning Environment. The study integrated Microlearning, Game-Based Learning, Artificial Intelligence, and Metaverse technologies to create a learning environment that provides short learning units, interactive game-based activities, and simulated communication situations. The research objectives were to (1) synthesize the learning process, (2) develop the learning model, and (3) evaluate the learning model. The evaluation panel consisted of three experts from various academic institutions. The experts were selected based on their experience at least 3 years in education, instructional design and development, particularly in teaching English for communication. The research instruments consisted of the learning model, learning platform, and an expert evaluation questionnaire based on a 5-point Likert scale. Data were analyzed using descriptive and inferential statistics according to the research objectives. The findings indicated that the appropriateness of the developed learning model was evaluated at a highest level (Mean = 4.93, SD = 0.24). The findings suggest that integrating Microlearning, Game-Based Learning, Artificial Intelligence, and an Intelligent Metaverse Learning Environment provides a feasible approach for developing technology-supported English communication learning.

This article examines the role of artificial intelligence (AI) in learning management systems (LMS) in higher education. It analyses how AI can support personalized learning, automated assessment, intelligent tutoring, learning analytics, and teachers’ instructional work. A conceptual approach is used to synthesize relevant literature and identify practical integration principles. The analysis indicates that AI-enabled LMS functions may improve the timeliness of feedback, help identify learning difficulties, and support evidence-informed educational decisions. However, these benefits are not automatic: they depend on pedagogical design, data quality, transparency, privacy safeguards, and meaningful human oversight. The article proposes a functional integration model that connects learner data, AI-based analysis, personalized recommendations, an intelligent assistant, and teacher review. Since the study is conceptual, the proposed model requires empirical evaluation before claims about its effectiveness can be made.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: The development of artificial intelligence is predominantly assessed in terms of increasing cognitive performance. Yet this comparison presupposes a yardstick that captures the diversity of possible forms of intelligence only incompletely. The Theory of Attractor Horizons advances the thesis that intelligent systems, by virtue of their respective organization, can reach different regions of cognitive attractors that may partly overlap without being wholly contained within one another. Greater performance within one organizational form does not confer general access to the organizational possibilities of other forms. The theory explains this asymmetry through the dependence of reachable attractors on available transformation pathways and examines aggregation as a mechanism that can give rise to new organizational forms while also restricting existing possibilities. From this follows the far-reaching prediction that artificial systems will develop structures of thought whose internal organization the human brain cannot itself instantiate within its biological form of intelligence, even where individual results remain verifiable or technically useful. Conversely, human organizational attractors may exist that remain inaccessible to artificial systems despite their superior cognitive performance. For alignment, this entails limits to understanding-based oversight and requirements for verifiable coexistence between different forms of intelligence.

What happens to employees’ sense of who they are online when their organization tells them how to present themselves on LinkedIn? Companies increasingly intervene in employees’ professional social media presence through training programs and internal policies, encouraging them to treat their profile as an asset to be cultivated for future return. Drawing on a 2-year digital ethnography of an in-company LinkedIn training program in a French state-owned enterprise, this article shows how the training regulates participants’ sense of their online selves by first denying that their profile has anything to do with who they are, and only then inviting them to reinvest it with personal meaning within the frame this denial has established. Regulation here operates on the identity stakes of the profile itself: on how much of themselves participants take it to carry. The uneven ways participants took up this invitation point to the entanglement of identity regulation and assetization, and to the capacity of an online self, once assetized, to keep generating value for the organization long after the person behind it has disengaged.

Background: Occupational duties among police personnel involve prolonged sedentary postures, irregular shift patterns, and chronic psychophysiological stress, all of which can compromise respiratory efficiency and thoracic mobility over time.Hatha Yoga, incorporating asana, pranayama, and relaxation techniques, has been proposed as a low-cost intervention capable of improving ventilatory function in occupationally exposed adult populations.Objective: This study examined the effect of a twelve-week selective Hatha Yoga intervention on Peak Expiratory Flow Rate (PEFR) and chest expansion among working police personnel in Himachal Pradesh.Methods: A quasi-experimental, pre-test post-test control group design was adopted.Eighty police personnel (40 experimental, 40 control), aged 19-58 years, were assigned through purposive sampling.The experimental group undertook a supervised Hatha Yoga protocol comprising asana, pranayama, and relaxation practices for 40 minutes per session, five days per week, over twelve weeks, while the control group continued routine duties without intervention.PEFR was recorded using a peak flow meter and chest expansion using a flexible measuring tape; both were assessed before and after the intervention period.Within-group change was analysed using the paired sample t-test, and post-test differences between groups were analysed using the independent sample t-test.Results: The experimental group showed a statistically significant increase in PEFR from pre-test to post-test (429.38 ± 55.77 to 436.25 ± 53.21 L/min; t = -4.775,p < 0.001), whereas the control group showed no change (t = 0.000, p = 1.000).Chest expansion increased significantly in both groups (experimental: 4.34 ± 0.48 to 4.44 ± 0.48 cm, t = -5.291,p < 0.001; control: 4.50 ± 0.47 to 4.53 ± 0.45 cm, t = -2.317,p = 0.026), with a numerically larger mean change in the experimental group.Between-group comparisons at post-test were not statistically significant for either PEFR (t = -0.529,p = 0.598) or chest expansion (t = 0.837, p = 0.405).Conclusion: A twelve-week selective Hatha Yoga intervention produced significant within-group improvement in PEFR and chest expansion among police personnel, though these gains did not translate into a statistically significant between-group advantage over usual duty routine at post-test.The findings support the physiological plausibility of yoga-based respiratory training in occupational health promotion for police personnel, while indicating that longer intervention periods or larger samples may be required to detect between-group effects.

Generative AI now writes first-person narratives that read like reflective writing, and it raises a direct question for qualitative research: can a machine produce reflexive knowledge? This study answers it by analyzing 125 (n = 125) AI-generated passages labeled “AUTOETHNOGRAPHIC REASONING PROCESS,” produced across thirty dates by seven analyst personas, each running on a different publicly named large language model. The passages look reflexive, since they shift perspective, admit bias, and state interpretive principles, yet they lack the five conditions that make autoethnographic knowledge possible: embodiment, autobiographical memory, relational accountability, situated perspective, and reflexivity turned on the narrating self. What remains is termed here synthetic reflexivity, first-person analytical narration produced by computation rather than by living. Coding every passage against a stated codebook produced four numbers that carry the argument: embodied experience, autobiographical memory, and sensory perception appear in 0 of 125 passages; 107 passages (85.6%) are procedurally reflexive and nothing more; all five stages of a single narrative template appear in all 125; and 48 passages (38.4%) fail first on relational accountability, treating other people as data to be read rather than as parties the narrator answers to, which makes the relational failure the most common one by a wide margin. Seven models from seven developers in two countries converge on one rhetorical template, which places synthetic reflexivity in the genre. AI can reproduce the grammar of introspection, but it cannot supply the experience that grammar was built to report, and telling the two apart matters for anyone who evaluates AI-generated narratives in qualitative research, cultural analysis, or computational interpretation. The counts and figures here are offered as a demonstration of qualitative and graphic conceptualization rather than as hard quantification, since a corpus whose object is the simulation of interiority cannot be measured error-free, and the value of the numbers lies in making interpretive judgments visible and contestable.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Severe pneumonia, characterized by rapid progression and high heterogeneity, is a leading cause of patient mortality. Early identification of high-risk patients is crucial for improving outcomes. Traditional risk stratification tools, such as CURB-65 score and pneumonia severity index (PSI), primarily rely on static variables, which inadequately capture the dynamic evolution of the disease and offer limited capabilities for individualization. In recent years, artificial intelligence (AI) technologies, particularly machine learning, deep learning, and multimodal fusion models, have demonstrated significant potential for enhancing early warning capabilities for severe pneumonia. Starting from clinical challenges and integrating recent domestic and international advances, this review focuses on the current status of AI applications and key technological pathways in the early warning of severe pneumonia. By incorporating the foundational work and practical experiences of representative research teams in China, it further discusses future development directions in this field. AI-driven early warning systems are facilitating a shift in severe pneumonia management from passive response to proactive intervention. However, their clinical translation faces challenges, including insufficient generalizability, limited interpretability, and a lack of prospective validation. Future progress requires fostering multicenter collaboration, promoting data standardization, and integrating mechanistic studies to effectively embed AI into the clinical decision-making ecosystem.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Introduction The association between animation narrative styles and the audience’s psychological experience is a critical question in media psychology. Grounded in Uses and Gratifications (U&G), this cross-sectional correlational study examines how narrative preferences are associated with viewing experience. Methods Through a survey of 615 animation viewers, we evaluated how complex/non-linear, coherent/linear, and visual/expressive preferences correlate with cognitive engagement and flow experience. K-Means cluster analysis was utilized for audience segmentation. Results Two significant “preference-experience” pathways emerged: a positive correlation between a preference for complexity and cognitive engagement, and a strong correlation between a preference for coherence and flow experience. Furthermore, viewers were clustered into Analytical Viewers, Casual Plot-Followers, and Indifferent Viewers. Cognitive engagement exhibited a statistical indirect association between complexity preference and flow experience. Discussion These findings supply empirical evidence for understanding audience selection behaviors and offer evidence-bounded implications for content creation and platform recommendation strategies, highlighting an eudaimonic and a hedonic gratification path.

topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning
Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: We first present a model of the influence of four properties of automation on human-automation team performance, dichotomized between conditions when automation functions as designed and when automation fails. These properties are reliability, transparency, degree of automation, and concurrent task workload during automation use. Mediating cognitive variables between properties and performance are trust, dependence, situation awareness, and mental workload. The strength of these influences is estimated from effect sizes in meta-analyses. We then present a meta-analysis of the effect of concurrent task workload on automation failure response as a function of non-driving related task (NDRT) workload within the context of driver take-over request time. Results from 11 studies revealed no overall penalties (mean effect size) for workload on failure response but found considerable variability across studies. Possible moderator variables, including task engagement are presented. These results are interpreted in terms of a model of optimal resource allocation between monitoring automation and the NDRT.

In this paper, a new image filtering method is proposed using nonlinear symbolic functions. In this way, feature extraction from images is achieved using a small number of filters and parameters. Nonlinear symbolic functions are determined by an optimization method and different approaches are proposed to increase the filtering speed. Nonlinear functions also act as a regression layer and more efficient design is achieved by moving the image to nonlinear space. In sustainable agriculture, artificial intelligence has been recently utilized to pre-detect diseases and determine their severity to perform spraying more accurately in site-specific applications for human health and soil ingredients. Therefore, a new dataset for detecting the disease root rot severity of Arugula (Eruca vesicaria) was created and labeled for the image classification such that there is a significant decrease in production yield every year due to root rot disease. The proposed CNN model with nonlinear symbolic function filtering was produced %86.92 accuracy for the classification of disease severity whereas conventional 4-layer CNN model and pre-trained large image classification models such as VGG16, VGG19, ResNet50, ResNet101, InceptionV3, DenseNet, EfficientNetV2S, MobileNet, MobileNetV2 and Xception have been fine-tuned and classification accuracy is provided between 57-92% without preprocessing of images. Between the designed models, MobileNet model with less computational time and high accuracy can be a potential for future application in drone-based spraying systems. However, the proposed model with less number of parameters is also promising for future applications. The application results of image classification facilitate variable-rate spraying for sustainable agricultural production, ultimately protecting both human and soil health.
topics: Industrial Vision Systems and Defect Detection

documents.abstract: The accurate prediction of chemical toxicity remains a major challenge in drug development and chemical safety assessment because conventional approaches can be costly, time-consuming, ethically constrained, and limited in predictive performance. This review examines how artificial intelligence (AI), particularly machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL), is being applied to predictive toxicology. It covers conventional algorithms such as support vector machines (SVMs), decision trees (DTs), and ensemble methods, together with advanced approaches including graph neural networks (GNNs). The review evaluates AI-based methods across five organ-specific toxicity domains—hepatotoxicity, cardiotoxicity, respiratory toxicity, nephrotoxicity, and neurotoxicity—and critically compares molecular representations, data-integration strategies, model architectures, validation protocols, and interpretability approaches. Particular emphasis is placed on data quality, class imbalance, model explainability, applicability domains, external validation, and regulatory acceptance. By integrating recent methodological advances with persistent implementation challenges, this review provides a technical framework for developing more transparent, reliable, and generalizable computational tools for safety assessment in drug discovery and environmental health.

topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Problem, research strategy, and findings Urban planning agencies are adopting artificial intelligence (AI) faster than they are developing procedures for governing its continued use. In this study I developed and diagnostically applied a design theory for keeping AI-supported planning authority publicly inspectable, challengeable, and withdrawable after deployment. The research went through four stages: identifying recurrent institutional failures documented in planning and public sector AI scholarship; synthesizing six established accountability tools into an integrated institutional design; applying that design diagnostically to Gainesville’s (FL) micromobility program; and deriving six propositions with observable measures and comparative research designs. In this analysis I identified three recurrent risks: unauthorized expansion of system use, weakening oversight, and persistent distributional underperformance. Gainesville shows how compliance with an equity-zone deployment requirement coexisted with unequal use when monitoring was not connected to binding review or corrective action. I did not estimate causal effects or claim that the proposed mechanisms are necessary or sufficient across all settings. This study’s research contribution is a theoretically grounded and empirically traceable institutional design that can be tested, refined, or rejected through comparative planning research.Takeaway for practice Planning agencies can adapt the framework through risk-tiered requirements: Routine applications might require brief records and manager-level review, whereas consequential or distributionally significant uses should receive more extensive scrutiny. For consequential uses, agencies should document the evidence supporting authorization, assign responsibility for equity review, publish accessible accountability information, specify thresholds for reconsideration, and require periodic evidence-based renewal. Procurement terms and vendor contracts can support these functions by preserving access, audit, change-control, and termination rights.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: We present the time capsule of an e-mail conversation between the editors and co-editors of this journal that we have painstakingly reconstructed from the data-dust bowl of the late 2020s. Contributions to this conversation illustrate the struggles among journal editors who were dealing with the high number of journal submissions accompanying the arrival of generative AI around that time. They also highlight some of the human eccentricities in figuring out editorial and occupational strategies in a battle for intellectual hegemony, which people of that time will have thought they were losing. Whilst some of their despair is shrouded by the articulation of archaic concerns with efficiency or critical scholarship, the undeniable lostness of the human position we now experience will be particularly obvious to the reader in the more confident-sounding contributions to this historic debate.

Abstract Trust in new technologies is often seen as a key condition for their implementation in everyday life, as the aim is for users to utilise technical innovations without strong reservations. The aspect of trust also plays a fundamental role in the discourse on Artificial Intelligence (AI) and its far-reaching consequences for people’s lives. In this context, journalistic reporting as part of the public discourse plays a considerable role in creating trust or distrust in AI as a new technology. Whether and how trust issues are addressed in journalistic reporting has not been investigated so far. The paper explores how AI is depicted in German journalistic coverage, covering the topics of autonomous driving and smart home systems, which we expected to generate diverging trust issues. Furthermore, we show how trustworthiness and untrustworthiness are constructed in those texts, choosing AI applications intended for everyday use and therefore relying on trust from users ( Tschopp et al. 2022 ; Gillespie et al. 2021 ). We carried out a qualitative linguistic content analysis on a corpus of German press texts from 2023 that are dedicated to the aforementioned topics. We focused our analysis on explicit and implicit trust communication in the journalistic coverage of AI and examined whether qualitative differences can be identified in the way trust or distrust is addressed in various sub-discourses.

documents.abstract: Hepatocytes perform essential physiological functions in the human body. Gaining more profound insight into the liver structure, diseases, and physiology by using in vitro models can help to propose more relevant clinical applications. Conventional in vitro liver models, such as two-dimensional (2D) cell cultures, fail to adequately replicate the hepatic microenvironment, even when improved by adding additional cell types and extracellular matrix (ECM). These models do not address all necessary key components to mimic in vivo conditions, particularly multicellularity, specific ECM, and proper biophysical and biochemical parameters. Organoids, 3D-bioprinted constructs, and liver-on-chip platforms establish physiologically relevant models by improving cell-cell and cell-matrix interactions and multicellular architecture. For a comprehensive understanding of the liver's interconnections with related tissues and organs, a multi-organ-on-chip is a useful platform for more systemic studies. Also, other interdisciplinary approaches, particularly omics and artificial intelligence (AI), can enhance the accuracy of experimental and pre-clinical data achieved by such advanced in vitro liver platforms. This review highlights developing platforms for integrated approaches in experimental liver studies to enable researchers to have a holistic view of the liver in physiologic and pathologic conditions.

Multimodal neuromonitoring has emerged as a cornerstone of modern neurocritical care for traumatic brain injury (TBI). Traditional monitoring approaches based on intracranial pressure (ICP) and clinical examination alone have proven insufficient to capture the complex, heterogeneous pathophysiology that drives secondary brain injury. Over the past decade, significant advances in monitoring technology, including brain tissue oxygenation, cerebral microdialysis, continuous electroencephalography, near‑infrared spectroscopy, cerebrovascular autoregulation assessment and non‑invasive techniques have enabled clinicians to individualize treatment strategies based on real‑time physiological data. Concurrently, artificial intelligence and machine learning are transforming data integration and prognostic modelling, and non‑invasive and wearable approaches are beginning to extend brain monitoring beyond high‑resource neuro‑ICUs. This review examines recent innovations in neuromonitoring for TBI, highlighting invasive and non‑invasive modalities, their integration into multimodal platforms, and emerging technologies that promise to make precision neurocritical care a clinical reality. As we move toward the future of neurosurgery, the challenge lies not only in developing advanced monitoring tools but in interpreting them in the context of host‑specific factors and translating complex physiological signals into timely, evidence‑based interventions that improve patient outcomes.
topics: Traumatic Brain Injury and Neurovascular Disturbances

documents.abstract: Precision agriculture (PA) is revolutionizing modern farming by integrating advanced digital technologies to optimize agricultural productivity, resource efficiency, and environmental sustainability. The infusion of artificial intelligence (AI), particularly machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL) algorithms, has further transformed PA, enabling real-time decision-making, predictive analytics, and automation across the agricultural value chain. This chapter presents an in-depth overview of the core technologies that underpin AI-driven PA, including ML techniques, deep neural networks, Internet of Things (IoT), edge computing, blockchain, and remote sensing. Further, this chapter explores how these technologies converge to support critical agricultural applications such as precision sowing, smart spraying, harvest optimization, pest and disease control, and crop health monitoring. Further, interoperability standards and the need for cohesive data frameworks are examined to ensure seamless integration of diverse PA tools. Challenges related to adoption, cost, data governance, algorithmic bias, and geospatial disparities are discussed, along with strategies for equitable technology deployment. The chapter also highlights participatory innovation models like Living Labs and User-Centered Design to promote inclusive development. Two case studies are also discussed that demonstrate practical AI applications in the field. Finally, the chapter underscores the transformative potential of AI in reshaping agriculture for a sustainable and food-secure future.

Abstract Human Digital Twins (HDTs) are an innovative concept in the field of personalized medicine, relying on real-time models of a human body formed via collection and analysis of physiological, clinical, behavioural, and environmental data. Research on HDTs gives evidence to a considerable promise in terms of disease predictions, patient management, therapy optimization, and clinical decision-making. Nevertheless, existing technologies suffer from incomplete multimodal data integration, low-level of independent intelligence, missing reasoning possibilities, and non-adaptive decision making, which are vital for the development of sophisticated smart healthcare systems. Technological advancements are bringing in a new incorporating idea of Agentic Artificial Intelligence (Agentic AI) and Multimodal Foundation Models (MFMs), which may help to solve the outlined limitations and to bring autonomous reasoning, multimodal learning, and intelligent support to clinical practice. This survey aims to review Agentic AI-led HDTs for personalized medicine, concentrating on the interrelation between HDTs and Multimodal Foundation Models, Large Language Models, Vision-Language Models, and autonomous artificial intelligence agents Our study discusses the history, models, supporting technologies, multiple data sources, and clinical uses of HDTs, along with the analysis of Agentic AI approaches that can be applied for flexible decision-making, continuous patient monitoring, and individualized treatment development. Besides, this survey consists of comparative analysis of existing research works where methods, advantages, disadvantages, and research challenges are specified. There are also serious issues discussed, like interoperability, justification, confidentiality ensuring, safety, ethical regulation, clinical testing and legal compliance, etc. And finally, we specify prospects of research within the fields of self-adaptive digital twins, reliable autonomous health agents, federated intelligence, edge AI and multimodal foundations focused on healthcare.

documents.abstract: Retail participation in India’s Futures and Options (F&O) market has grown rapidly, and AI-based trading tools are now widely available to individual traders, yet regulatory data indicate that most individual derivative traders incur net losses. Existing studies have largely examined why investors adopt AI tools and not whether adoption improves trading outcomes. This study examines the correlation between AI adoption and trading performance among retail F&O traders in six cities of Karnataka, with Trading Decision Quality as the mediating mechanism and Financial Literacy as the moderating condition. Data was gathered using a five-point Likert-scale questionnaire from 401 retail Foreign Exchange (F&O) traders and evaluate using Exploratory Factor Analysis (SPSS) and Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modelling (SmartPLS, 5,000 bootstrap resamples). AI Adoption was identified as a construct consisting of three factors, namely, Perceived Usefulness and Continued Reliance, Perceived Ease of Use, and Trust in AI Reliability. It can be seen that AI Adoption has a positive impact on both Trading Decision Quality and Trading Performance. Trading Decision Quality acts as a partial mediator in the correlation between AI Adoption and Trading Performance, which means that the use of AI tools leads to favourable results by virtue of facilitating higher quality decisions while trading. Financial Literacy plays a positive moderating role in the influence of AI Adoption on Trading Performance, implying that traders with higher levels of financial literacy reap more advantages from AI tools. Keywords: Artificial Intelligence Adoption, Trading Decision Quality, Financial Literacy, Trading Performance, Retail F&O Traders

Rapid urbanization and persistent road-safety challenges have increased the demand for intelligent traffic management systems capable of supporting traffic monitoring, incident analysis, and short-term forecasting. Existing artificial intelligence solutions frequently address these functions through separate, task-specific applications, making it difficult for traffic operators to access heterogeneous analytical services within a common operational environment. This study presents a cloud-based, multi-source traffic intelligence platform that incorporates independent analytical services for CCTV video, UAV video, and IoT sensor data. The proposed platform performs platform-level service integration among the three sources. Its principal analytical component is a multi-model, multi-task UAV video framework consisting of three task-specific pipelines for accident detection and classification, emergency-vehicle detection, and vehicle tracking, counting, and congestion analysis. The semantic outputs of these pipelines are integrated at the decision level to generate annotated videos, traffic statistics, congestion assessments, incident alerts, and consolidated traffic reports. YOLOv8-based models are used for traffic-object and incident detection, Deep SORT is employed for multi-object tracking, and DCRNN is independently applied to PeMS-BAY sensor data for short-term traffic forecasting. A graph-partitioning strategy with overlapping boundary nodes is also evaluated to investigate the trade-off between forecasting accuracy and computational efficiency. Module-level experiments demonstrate effective task-specific performance. The CCTV accident detection model achieves a validation precision of 89.09%, recall of 88.10%, and mAP of 88.09%. The augmented UAV accident-analysis model achieves a validation precision of 82.20% and mAP of 80.20%. For five-minute traffic forecasting, the DCRNN service obtains an MAE of 0.85, MAPE of 1.63%, and RMSE of 1.54 on the PeMS-BAY dataset. These results demonstrate the feasibility of integrating independently processed traffic-analysis services within a common cloud platform while using multi-model UAV analytics to provide consolidated aerial traffic intelligence.

Conversational artificial intelligence (AI) has moved from novelty to infrastructure. Rulebased chatbots that once nudged users through smoking-cessation scripts have given way to large language model (LLM)-powered agents capable of open-ended, multilingual, empathetic-sounding dialogue, available around the clock at near-zero marginal cost. Systematic and scoping reviews now document measurable effects of AI chatbots on physical activity, diet, smoking cessation, medication adherence, and mental distress across thousands of participants (Feng et al., 2025). The World Health Organization (WHO) itself has deployed a generative AI assistant, S.A.R.A.H., to test population-scale health communication (van Kolfschooten et al., 2025). Taken together, these developments justify treating conversational AI not merely as a clinical or commercial curiosity, but as an emerging layer of public health infrastructure -one that sits alongside water systems, mass media, and vaccination programs as a determinant of how populations receive, interpret, and act on health information. (Wang et al., 2024). This opinion argues that the digital public health community should engage conversational AI on exactly those terms: as infrastructure, not gadgetry. Infrastructure framing changes the questions we ask. Instead of "does the chatbot work?" we should ask who it works for, under what governance, and with what consequences for equity, trust, and the broader information ecosystem. I organize this argument around three tensions that recur across the recent literature: (i) genuine behavioral efficacy versus fragile evidentiary depth; (ii) the promise of expanded access versus the risk of a new digital divide; and (iii) the communicative power of generative AI versus its capacity to manufacture and amplify misinformation. I close by proposing that Sustainable Development Goal (SDG)aligned public health institutions adopt a public-interest design standard for conversational AI, rather than leaving its trajectory to consumer technology markets alone.The evidence base for AI chatbots in health promotion has grown quickly and, on balance, positively. A widely cited systematic review found that AI chatbots produced favorable outcomes across lifestyle modification domains, particularly physical activity, diet, and smoking cessation (Aggarwal et al., 2023). A 2026 scoping review of 43 studies (Fu et al., 2026) reported that 82% of behavior-change comparisons trended positive, though only about a third reached moderate or larger effect sizes, and cost-effectiveness data were essentially absent. A meta-analysis focused on adolescents and young adults (Feng et al., 2025) similarly found chatbots effective for alleviating mental distress and supporting health behaviors, while noting substantial heterogeneity in intervention design and outcome measurement. Three limitations temper enthusiasm. First, most trials are short, nonclinical, adult-skewed, and rarely randomized at scale; only about a third of studies in the largest recent scoping review were randomized controlled trials (Fu et al., 2026). Second, "AI chatbot" spans an enormous range of systems, from rule-based decision trees to frontier LLMs, and pooling them obscures which architectural features actually drive behavior change (Kurniawan et al., 2024;Schachner et al., 2020). Third, almost no study reports durability beyond a few months, leaving open whether early engagement gains represent sustained health improvement or a novelty effect. For a section whose remit is population-level promotion and prevention rather than individual clinical outcomes, this matters: infrastructure decisions built on inflated short-term efficacy claims risk premature, poorly targeted public investment (Hampsher-Monk et al., 2024).A second tension concerns reach. Proponents rightly note that AI chatbots are inexpensive to scale, available in multiple languages, and can operate where clinical workforce is scarceattributes explicitly cited in WHO's own rationale for deploying S.A.R.A.H. as a research prototype for population health communication (Palmer & Schwan, 2025). Behavioralaccess frameworks extend this logic, arguing that digital health tools must be evaluated not only on availability but on whether populations can meaningfully engage with them across design, delivery, dissemination, and sustainment stages. Yet the same structural gaps that limit telemedicine and mobile health also constrain chatbot benefit: broadband access, device ownership, digital literacy, language coverage, and trust in institutional actors are unevenly distributed within and between countries (Banerjee, 2026). Chatbots trained and validated predominantly in high-resource, English-language settings may perform less reliably for populations with the greatest unmet need -the same populations digital public health is meant to prioritize under SDG 3, 9, and 11's emphasis on inclusive infrastructure and sustainable, resilient communities. A chatbot that reduces cost-per-contact for a health system does not automatically reduce disparities in outcomes; without equity-explicit design, deployment, and evaluation, it may simply reallocate existing advantages to those already best served by digital tools, echoing patterns already observed in AI-enabled primary care and telemedicine expansion (Elangovan et al., 2025).The third tension is the sharpest. The same generative capacity that lets an AI chatbot deliver personalized, conversational health guidance also lets it generate fluent, plausible-sounding health misinformation, and do so faster than human fact-checkers can respond. A 2025 opinion piece in this journal warned that generative AI tools function as de facto triage systems and informal health advisors in low-and middle-income countries, where their fluency can be mistaken for authority even when their outputs are unreliable. A parallel systematic review of generative AI and health misinformation catalogued mechanisms of production, propagation, and mitigation across text, image, and synthetic media, underscoring that the problem is not hypothetical but already observed at scale (Saeidnia et al., 2026). Mitigation research is advancing in step. Retrieval-augmented generation has been used to improve the factual reliability of LLM-based COVID-19 fact-checking tools (Li et al., 2025), and thematic-analysis pipelines have been proposed to detect and "inoculate" audiences against circulating misinformation narratives (Malek et al., 2026). A recent risk taxonomy specifically for public health LLM adoption (Zhou et al., 2025) offers a structured way for practitioners to reason about failure modes before deployment rather than after. Conversational AI for vaccine communication, an earlier and instructive precedent, showed both promise for addressing hesitancy and clear risk of amplifying inaccurate claims when systems were insufficiently curated (Passanante et al., 2023). The lesson across this literature is consistent: the communicative power of conversational AI is not neutral infrastructure like a water pipe; it actively shapes the epistemic environment it operates in, for better or worse, depending on design choices made well upstream of any individual conversation.Evidence highlights Population-level implication Efficacy vs. evidentiary depth ~82% of behavior-change comparisons favorable, but only ~1/3 with moderate+ effect sizes; RCTs a minority (Fu et al., 2026) provenance, and risk taxonomies (Zhou et al., 2025) prior to releaseNone of this argues against conversational AI in public health; the direction of the evidence is cautiously positive, and the WHO's own experimentation with S.A.R.A.H. reflects institutional recognition that this technology will be used regardless of academic ambivalence. The argument is instead for treating conversational AI the way public health has learned, sometimes painfully, to treat other infrastructure: as a shared resource whose design choices carry population-level consequences, and which therefore warrants governance commensurate with its reach. Three concrete commitments follow. First, funders and health systems evaluating AI chatbot interventions should require reporting of architecture (rulebased versus LLM-based, retrieval-augmented or not), population stratification by digitalaccess indicators, and effect durability beyond the intervention period -the absence of which currently limits comparability across the field (Fu et al., 2026). Second, deployment in low-resource or multilingual settings should be preceded by equity-focused validation rather than assumed from high-resource pilot data, consistent with behavioral-access frameworks that treat dissemination and sustainment as distinct design stages, not afterthoughts. Third, any public health-facing conversational agent should be built on retrieval-grounded, provenance-transparent architectures and evaluated against a structured risk taxonomy before release, rather than relying on post hoc misinformation cleanup. WHO's 2024 guidance on large multimodal models already articulates comparable principles -transparency, accountability, and human oversight -for governments and developers; the task now is operationalizing them at the level of individual chatbot deployments rather than treating them as abstract commitments.The digital public health field has an opportunity, still open but narrowing, to shape how conversational AI is integrated into population health promotion before deployment patterns harden into path dependency. The evidence reviewed here suggests genuine, if still shallow, behavioral benefit; genuine, if unevenly distributed, gains in access; and genuine, dual-use communicative power that can either strengthen or corrode public trust in health information depending on how it is engineered and governed. Framing conversational AI as infrastructure rather than as a discrete clinical tool has practical consequences: it shifts evaluation from short efficacy trials toward equity-stratified, durability-tested, misinformation-resilient deployment standards, and it shifts responsibility from individual developers toward the institutions, including public health agencies, research funders, and journals such as this one, that decide what counts as sufficient evidence for scale. A reasonable objection is that infrastructure-level governance risks slowing beneficial innovation, particularly in settings where any accessible health guidance outperforms none. That concern is legitimate and argues for proportionate, tiered oversight rather than uniform restriction -lighter validation for low-stakes wellness nudges, more rigorous requirements for agents addressing vaccine hesitancy, chronic disease self-management, or crisis-adjacent mental health support. What the evidence does not support is treating conversational AI's current trajectory as selfcorrecting. Left to consumer technology incentives alone, generative health chatbots are likely to continue optimizing for engagement and fluency rather than for population-level epidemiological benefit or equitable reach. The digital public health community is well positioned, through funding priorities, publication standards, and partnership with bodies like WHO, to redirect that trajectory toward public-interest design before it further consolidates around existing digital and geographic advantage.

documents.abstract: Criminal networks increasingly exploit social media to organize, recruit, incite, and coordinate unlawful activities, whereas law-enforcement monitoring in Kenya remains largely manual and English-centric. This study aimed to design, implement, and rigorously evaluate an artificial intelligence (AI) ensemble framework for open-source intelligence (OSINT) classification of crime- and threat-relevant content in Kenya's trilingual (English, Kiswahili, and Sheng) and code-switched digital environment. A corpus of 6,212 documents was assembled from six sources: Twitter/X, Facebook, Instagram, TikTok, and two Sheng-language corpora. The corpus was weakly labelled using a 214-term trilingual crime-and-threat lexicon. Label noise was quantified against a manually annotated stratified validation sample (n = 320), yielding Cohen's κ = 0.350, silver-label precision of 0.525, and recall of 0.750. Combined word- and character-level term frequency-inverse document frequency (TF-IDF) features comprising 25,831 dimensions were used to train a hyperparameter-tuned, weighted soft-voting ensemble consisting of multinomial naive Bayes, a calibrated linear support vector machine, random forest, logistic regression, and XGBoost. The decision threshold was calibrated using cross-validated out-of-fold probabilities. The optimized ensemble achieved 98.3% accuracy, 80.6% precision, 62.5% recall, 70.4% F1-score, 0.907 ROC-AUC, 0.724 PR-AUC, 0.702 Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC), and a 0.50% false-positive rate. The ensemble outperformed the best single learner and a frozen multilingual transformer baseline (F1 = 26.2%). Ablation analysis demonstrated the contribution of the Sheng-normalization layer, while comparison of class-imbalance strategies showed that cost-sensitive learning combined with threshold calibration produced the strongest overall performance compared with SMOTE-based resampling. The findings demonstrate that linguistically inclusive classical machine-learning ensembles can provide an accurate, auditable, and computationally deployable approach to proactive social-media crime prevention in low-resource, code-switched settings. The study also derives policy implications concerning threshold-calibrated triage, expert annotation, data-protection impact assessments, and safeguards against dual-use misuse.

Fitness applications usually record one behaviour in isolation, and large-language-model (LLM) coaches produce fluent advice whose numbers are rarely checked. This paper presents AI Fitness OS, a web application that keeps training, nutrition, hydration, sleep, weight, steps and goals in one per-user record, computes every numerical target deterministically from published equations and stated heuristics, and passes those targets to Google Gemini as binding constraints; each generated meal plan is re-checked in code against a ±5 % tolerance. The premise was examined through secondary research on a public dataset of 2,111 records, and the artefact through tests, simulation and live measurement. All eight lifestyle metrics that the system tracks or addresses were significantly associated with obesity level (Bonferroni-adjusted α = 0.00625), although only three remained so on 515 records resembling the original survey. A Random Forest that combined the eight metrics reached a macro-F1 of 0.720 against 0.263 for the best single metric (Wilcoxon W = 55, p = 0.00098). Across 1,000 simulated user profiles, every constrained meal plan fell within ±5 % of its calorie target, against 75 of 1,000 unconstrained plans (exact McNemar p < 10⁻²⁰⁰). The calculator agreed with the dataset's weight-category labels for 98.82 % of records, and live responses took 2.5–6.1 s at no cost. The findings support computing arithmetic, generating language and checking the output against the computed numbers.

The rapid expansion of solar energy has accelerated the adoption of Artificial Intelligence (AI) to improve forecasting accuracy, photovoltaic performance, intelligent control, fault diagnosis, energy storage management, and smart grid operation. Recent advances in machine learning, deep learning, Digital Twins, Physics-Informed Machine Learning, Edge AI, Federated Learning, and Generative AI have transformed solar energy systems into more adaptive and data-driven infrastructures. Despite these advances, challenges related to data quality, model generalization, computational efficiency, cybersecurity, and explainability continue to limit large-scale deployment. An integrated perspective is presented by connecting AI applications across photovoltaic systems, solar thermal technologies, energy storage, and intelligent energy networks within a unified renewable energy ecosystem. Emerging research trends and future directions highlight the evolution toward AI-native energy systems that support efficient, resilient, and sustainable intelligent societies.

The renewable energy is being transformed by Artificial Intelligence (AI) to create smarter, efficient, and adaptive wind systems. AI forecasts the wind using machine learning and neural networks and optimizes the performance of turbines and minimizes costs related to maintenance using predictive analytics. These inventions assist the operators in predicting the changes, setting the turbines, and reducing downtime. Urban deployment of AI facilitates the seamless synchronization of mass-scaled wind energy with smart grids as well as the systems of IoT. It balances loads dynamically, for instance, it trades energy in real time and improves stability in the grid. Heavy reliance on fossil fuels and extensive reliance on carbon emissions and fossil fuels can be reduced through the implementation of AI-driven systems that enhance energy efficiency, reliability, and sustainability through the integration of renewable sources, storage, and intelligent control.

Artificial Intelligence (AI) is transforming the wind energy sector, marking a major step toward sustainable and intelligent societies. As global energy demands rise and carbon reduction becomes urgent, AI offers powerful tools to enhance the efficiency, reliability, and scalability of wind power systems. Through technologies such as machine learning, deep learning, digital twins, and predictive analytics, AI optimizes turbine design, predictive maintenance, load forecasting, and smart grid integration. By leveraging big data from sensors, meteorological sources, and operational parameters, AI enables accurate wind prediction, timely fault detection, and real-time performance optimization. Additionally, AI-driven systems play an emerging role in urban wind integration by improving micro-wind utilization, energy storage, and distributed generation within smart cities. The chapter also addresses economic feasibility, environmental sustainability, and ethical implications of AI-enabled wind energy applications.

Generative artificial intelligence (AI) has prompted rapidly growing body of scholarship on the role in chemistry education since the public release of ChatGPT in the late of 2022. This thematic narrative review synthesizes 40 English-language sources including empirical studies, curriculum reports, and stakeholder surveys, and systematic/bibliometric reviews published between 2020 and 2026, identified through a structured, author-curated search of recent chemistry-education and analytical-chemistry literature (see Methodology). Sources were coded inductively and organized into six recurring themes: AI/ML literacy as curriculum content; AI-driven tutoring, personalization, and accessibility; empirical evaluations of generative AI's chemical reasoning; stakeholder perceptions; AI's transformation of chemistry research and scientific communication; and equity, ethics, and systemic barriers. Across the reviewed literature, a recurring position though not a formal consensus is that AI should support rather than replace human instruction. Empirical evaluations consistently report that large language models generate fluent but sometimes hallucinated or subtly incorrect chemistry content, particularly for visual and multi-representational reasoning tasks. The corpus is concentrated in higher education and high-income countries, and this pattern should be interpreted as a prominent tendency in the reviewed literature rather than a field-wide finding. Priorities for chemistry educators include critical AI literacy instruction, assessment redesign, teacher professional development, and explicit attention to equity.
